title: Chapter 6 Mastery Quiz: Endocrine System, Circadian Rhythms & Sleep
description: Test your mastery of the HPA axis, cortisol regulation, the SCN master clock, sleep architecture, glymphatic clearance, and sleep disorders.

questions.question: What is the primary master clock governing circadian rhythms in the mammalian brain?

options.text: Suprachiasmatic Nucleus (SCN) of the anterior hypothalamus

questions.explanation: The SCN in the hypothalamus contains cell-autonomous molecular pacemakers that synchronize internal circadian timing.

questions.question: In the HPA stress axis, what hormone is secreted by the hypothalamus to stimulate ACTH release from the anterior pituitary?
questions.explanation: CRH is synthesized in the paraventricular nucleus of the hypothalamus and triggers pituitary ACTH secretion.

questions.question: Which endocrine gland synthesizes and secretes the primary glucocorticoid stress hormone Cortisol?
questions.explanation: The adrenal cortex (specifically the zona fasciculata) secretes cortisol in response to circulating ACTH.

questions.question: What is the biological effect of chronic elevated cortisol on hippocampal CA3/CA1 pyramidal neurons?

options.text: Dendritic retraction, loss of spines, and neurotoxic vulnerability
Increased synaptic resistance to glutamate excitotoxicity

questions.explanation: Chronic hypercortisolemia causes dendritic atrophy and synaptic loss in the hippocampus, impairing negative feedback shut-off.

questions.question: What natural environmental cue is the primary Zeitgeber for entraining the human master circadian clock?
questions.explanation: Light is the predominant Zeitgeber that entrains human circadian rhythms via the retinohypothalamic tract.

questions.question: Intrinsically Photosensitive Retinal Ganglion Cells (ipRGCs) are most sensitive to which wavelength spectrum of light?
questions.explanation: Melanopsin in ipRGCs exhibits peak absorption around 480 nm (blue light spectrum).

questions.question: Which endocrine gland synthesizes Melatonin under the regulatory control of the SCN?
questions.explanation: The pineal gland converts serotonin into melatonin during nocturnal darkness, signaling biological night.

questions.question: Which brain waves predominate during calm, relaxed wakefulness with eyes closed?
questions.explanation: Alpha oscillations emerge prominently over the occipital cortex when an individual rests quietly with eyes shut.

questions.question: What are Sleep Spindles in polysomnography?

options.text: Brief 11-16 Hz bursts of rhythmic EEG activity generated by the thalamus during Stage N2 sleep
Sudden violent muscle contractions of the legs during REM sleep
Slow delta waves of less than 1 Hz in Stage N3 sleep
Artifacts produced by cardiac pacemaker leads

questions.explanation: Sleep spindles are 11-16 Hz bursts generated by the thalamic reticular nucleus in N2 sleep that aid memory consolidation.

questions.question: What is the primary function of K-complexes observed during Stage N2 sleep?

options.text: Protecting sleep continuity by suppressing cortical processing of non-threatening environmental noises
Stimulating saliva secretion to prevent dry mouth
Accelerating heart rate during intense nightmare dreams

questions.explanation: K-complexes provide isolated cortical down-states that protect sleep continuity from disruptive ambient sounds.

questions.question: Stage N3 Slow-Wave Sleep (SWS) is electrophysiologically characterized by which prominent waves?

options.text: High-amplitude, ultra-slow Delta waves (0.5 to 4 Hz)
Rapid, low-voltage Beta waves (15 to 25 Hz)
Continuous absence of any electrical voltage

questions.explanation: Stage N3 (deep slow-wave sleep) requires delta waves occupying more than 20% of an epoch.

questions.question: During which sleep stage does the highest surge of human Growth Hormone (GH) release occur?
questions.explanation: Pulsatile secretion of growth hormone peaks sharply during slow-wave sleep (N3), supporting tissue repair and protein synthesis.

questions.question: What is the biological mechanism preventing people from physically acting out their dreams during REM sleep?

options.text: Active motor atonia driven by pontine inhibitory projections using glycine and GABA to paralyze spinal motor neurons
Total exhaustion of ATP inside muscle fibers
Temporary disconnection of the optic nerves from the thalamus
Complete closure of the spinal central canal

questions.explanation: REM sleep atonia is mediated by pontine subcoeruleus neurons projecting to spinal inhibitory interneurons, hyperpolarizing motor neurons.

questions.question: In the Glymphatic System discovered by Nedergaard, which astrocytic water channel facilitates bulk flow of CSF through brain tissue?
questions.explanation: Aquaporin-4 channels clustered on perivascular astrocyte end-feet facilitate convective CSF-interstitial fluid exchange.

questions.question: By what percentage does the brain's interstitial space expand during deep Slow-Wave Sleep to flush metabolic debris?
questions.explanation: Nedergaard et al. proved that interstitial space increases by ~60% during natural sleep, reducing hydrodynamic resistance.

questions.question: What neurotoxic peptides are actively cleared from brain parenchyma by the glymphatic system during sleep?
questions.explanation: Glymphatic clearance flushes out metabolic waste products including amyloid-beta and tau, which otherwise form Alzheimer's pathology.

questions.question: The Synaptic Homeostasis Hypothesis (Tononi & Cirelli) posits that a core function of sleep is to:

options.text: Downscale overall synaptic strength to baseline levels to restore energy balance and prevent network saturation
Increase every synapse in the cortex by 10-fold
Eliminate all glial astrocytes from the cortex

questions.explanation: The SHY hypothesis proposes that slow-wave sleep renormalizes net synaptic weight increases accumulated during waking learning.

questions.question: Narcolepsy with Cataplexy is caused by the autoimmune loss of neurons producing which neuropeptide?
questions.explanation: Narcolepsy Type 1 is caused by selective destruction of ~70,000 orexin/hypocretin neurons in the lateral hypothalamus.

questions.question: What is Cataplexy in patients with Narcolepsy?

options.text: Sudden, temporary loss of voluntary muscle tone triggered by strong emotions while consciousness is preserved
A severe convulsive seizure occurring during swimming
Total inability to open the eyes upon waking

questions.explanation: Cataplexy involves sudden intrusion of REM atonia into wakefulness, typically provoked by laughing, joy, or surprise.

questions.question: REM Sleep Behavior Disorder (RBD) is of immense diagnostic importance because it represents a strong early prodrome for:

options.text: Alpha-synucleinopathies such as Parkinson's disease and Dementia with Lewy Bodies

questions.explanation: Loss of REM atonia causing violent dream enactment precedes clinical motor signs of Parkinson's disease in up to 80-90% of cases.

questions.question: How long is a typical human ultradian NREM-REM sleep cycle in healthy adults?
questions.explanation: Adults cycle through NREM and REM stages roughly every 90-110 minutes, repeating 4-5 times per night.

questions.question: What is the primary underlying pathophysiology of Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA)?

options.text: Repeated mechanical collapse and obstruction of the upper pharyngeal airway during sleep leading to hypoxemia and micro-arousals
Complete failure of the diaphragm muscle due to spinal trauma
Excessive accumulation of CSF in the fourth ventricle

questions.explanation: Pharyngeal airway collapse blocks airflow, triggering nocturnal oxygen desaturations, sympathetic surges, and sleep fragmentation.
